name: Broch of Mousa
about: Mousa Broch, on a low rock promontory on the west shore of the island of Mousa, Shetland, is the best-preserved Iron Age broch: a drystone tower of local Old Red Sandstone flags, about 15 m across at the base and 12 m at the top, still standing 13.3 m high. The lower part of the wall is solid apart from three cells (beehive chambers), three recesses in the court wall and the stair entrance. Above that the wall is hollow: an inner and an outer wall tied together by floors of large slabs that make six galleries, one above another. A stair rises through the galleries to the wall-head. Four vertical sets of openings (voids) light the galleries from the court, and two scarcement ledges run round the court wall. Its date is given as about 300 BC (Wikipedia, HES on Sketchfab), the last century BC to first century AD (Hamilton 1970), or 100 BC to AD 150 (Thomas 2011). Later a wheelhouse-type inner wall with radial partitions, a bench, a tank and a hearth were built in the court. Norse sagas use it as a refuge in about AD 900 and in 1153. Changes: the court was cleared in 1861 (repairs then too). A higher doorway put in before 1851 was taken out in 1919, when the Office of Works cleared the court, surveyed the broch, pinned loose stones, bedded the top stones and lowered the entrance lintel to its original height. Part of the wall-head is reconstructed, and there was more stabilisation from 1967 into the 1980s. The 'now' view should have the 1919 entrance and the reconstructed wall-head; the 'as built' view has the original passage with its chamber above and no secondary court walling.

phases.what: Court cleared to the original floor and sill. Outside ground lowered to the rock. Full survey made. Loose stones pinned, top stones bedded down, entrance lintel lowered to its original height.

cites.quote: the lowering of the lintel over the entrance doorway to its original height
The ground round the exterior of the broch was lowered to the foundation level
Major stabilisation was undertaken between 1967 and the 1980s

phases.name: Laser scan
phases.what: 3D laser scan by Archaeoptics Ltd for Historic Scotland

cites.quote: in 2005 archaeologists used 3D laser scanning to document the structure
Produced from 2004 laser scan data by Archaoeoptics Ltd.

debate.claim: Roofed or open court. Did the scarcements carry a timber roundhouse, timber floors or galleries, scaffolding, or nothing? No post-holes or roof material have been found, and Thomas and Dryden argue for an open court. Graham argued the lower scarcement carried a balcony, not a roof. Paterson suggested the bench area was roofed with stone slabs.

cites.quote: It has recently been argued that the scarcements may have supported scaffolding in a roofless building.
the lower one at least must have supported a balcony and not a roof
no evidence of supporting roof structures is apparent
it is probable that this space was covered by stone flags and that no timber was used

debate.claim: Mousa is not a typical broch. Its ground plan is exceptionally small and massive (64.5% wall base), and its continuous stair is unique.

cites.quote: Mousa is a broch of ordinary wall-construction for Shetland, but built to an exceptionally restricted ground-plan
The only unique architectural feature at Mousa is one often regarded as standard to all brochs

debate.claim: What the galleries were for. Most see them as structural or used while building, not living space. The stair shows little wear.

cites.quote: They were probably used by the builders as an aid to constructing the building, rather than for accommodation or storage.
the greatest use was made during the construction of the building when they might have made it easier to haul stonework to the upper courses

debate.claim: The curved (ogee) profile: deliberate batter (Hamilton) or settlement and slipping of the outer wall (Dryden; HES: 'may have been accentuated by settlement')? See facts.profile_batter.

cites.quote: It is certain that this form is the result of accident

debate.claim: Is the stair continuous? Paterson: broken by a landing at the second gallery, against Dryden. Hamilton: 'ascends without interruption' with a landing above the second scarcement. Fojut: continuous apart from a short landing.

cites.quote: does not run in one continuous flight as indicated by Dryden

plans.what it shows: General plan, sections and an unrolled elevation of the stair and galleries. Paterson says it has some errors in parts not dimensioned.

gaps: The HES Statement of Significance, the HES property pages (historicenvironment.scot) and Canmore/trove.scot (site 944, with the RCAHMS 1946 Inventory text: about 50 ft base, 40 ft top, 15 ft wall) could not be used. historicenvironment.scot returns HTTP 429 to the checker, and canmore.org.uk now redirects to trove.scot, which sits behind an Azure WAF JavaScript challenge. The RCAHMS Inventory (1946, vol. 3, no. 1206) and the Statement of Significance figures are not quoted.

The 2004/2005 laser scan (Archaeoptics for Historic Scotland) has not been published as open data. HES's Sketchfab model has no licence and cannot be downloaded. No 'Scottish Ten' scan of Mousa was found; that programme scanned the World Heritage Sites.
Wall thickness higher up the tower (inner and outer skins separately) is not given as numbers in any source reached. Use Paterson's fig. 4 sections and the gallery widths.
The gallery floor heights in Thomas's Table 3 do not fit the 13.3 m height (gallery 6 at 14.02 m). The real levels need Paterson's fig. 4 or Hamilton's section, read to scale.
The stair's rise and tread (Dryden) are unreadable in the OCR. The total number of steps and exactly where the stair comes out at the wall-head were not found.
Which of Paterson's letters A, B, C is which cell is shown only on his plan. The text gives no orientation for them.
No radiocarbon date for Mousa. The task's 'about 400-100 BC' is not in any source reached; the sources give c. 300 BC, the 1st century BC to 1st century AD, or 100 BC-AD 150.
The Shetland Amenity Trust and the Mousa RSPB reserve pages were not checked. Storm petrel numbers are quoted from Wikipedia only (6,800 pairs on the island).
